segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Chana Joffe-Walt, sitting in for Ira Glass. So a couple of weeks ago, I was calling principals and teachers to find out what it was like to be in schools.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I called Principal Brian Cox in Wyoming. Did he have a minute to talk?

segments.speaker: Brian Cow
segments.text: Um, I can, yeah. I've got to be out on bus duty in, like, 15 minutes.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Principal Cox normally does not do bus duty. He also does not normally teach French class, because he's a principal, and he doesn't know French. He did both the week we spoke, because 20% of his staff were absent. Omicron.

segments.speaker: Brian Cow
segments.text: You know, I told somebody today when we walked in-- we had three paraprofessionals down in very key special education classrooms-- and I told them our goal today is to be a hockey goalie and just keep it out of the net.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Two things I learned from calling around to lots of educators over the last few weeks-- school is still a mess. That's the first thing. And number two, the situation in schools right now can only be described using metaphor.

segments.speaker: Brian Cow
segments.text: We're just going to play for eight hours today and try to keep as few of them from getting by us today. And then we'll recoup tonight and figure out how we can recover for tomorrow.

segments.speaker: Amy Gallaway
segments.text: Oh, man. This year-- [CHUCKLES] I'll try not to cry. This year has been hard. [CHUCKLES]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Amy Gallaway, a teacher in Alaska, says, I thought this year was finally going to be normal. This year is not.

segments.speaker: Amy Gallaway
segments.text: Like a creaky, creaky bridge that we're trying to get across.

segments.speaker: Math Teacher
segments.text: The kind of step where you're not going to die, you're going to roll your ankle.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: A math teacher in New York City.

segments.speaker: Math Teacher
segments.text: And land with your face in a mud puddle and be like, OK, I could have probably navigated that obstacle a little bit differently.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: There are not enough teachers. There are not enough school bus drivers. You never know which students will come in person, if at all. Some kids have just disappeared. Enrollment and attendance-- way down.

segments.speaker: Takeru Nagayoshi
segments.text: The metaphor that I would always use is like, it's as though you are creating a vehicle--

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You can tell this guy is about to go in really deep, right? English teacher.

segments.speaker: Takeru Nagayoshi
segments.text: --while driving it at the same time on a road whose conditions are unclear in terrible weather. That vehicle, by the way, is a school bus. And not only are there 120 kids there, you're also driving from the back of the bus.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: [LAUGHS] That's a metaphor that never ends.

segments.speaker: English Teacher
segments.text: Yeah. It just compounds.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Takeru Nagayoshi, a high school teacher in New Bedford, Massachusetts. Mr. Nagayoshi was Massachusetts teacher of the year for 2020. In 2021, he quit his job-- quit his job, right after being publicly recognized as the very best.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: He was at the top of his game, and he walked away, which is a pretty huge reversal. He didn't plan to leave public school teaching. When schools closed and everything went online, Mr. Nagayoshi missed the classroom deeply. He missed all the things you can only do when everyone is in a room together.

segments.speaker: Takeru Nagayoshi
segments.text: The group activities, the collaborative mood board work that my kids do, writing on anchor charts, breaking up into small groups, doing practice rounds of public speaking, and Socratic seminars, and peer writing, and taking out your pens so that you can highlight things on your papers, and give that feedback, and offer commentary to each other's research questions. And there are so many opportunities and magic that I think happens in person. And when I think about learning, it's such a social thing.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: He was used to feeling inspired every day, energized. But even when they were back in person, Mr. Nagayoshi never got that feeling back. His students didn't get to school on time or regularly at all. And they just weren't focused.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: They were grieving for people they loved. They were stressed or depressed, juggling lots of responsibilities, or staying up until 4:00 AM playing video games. And they were just out of the habit of doing school. School had been such a regular routine before, for kids, for everyone.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Mr. Nagayoshi told me he started to question if what they were doing was really serving kids. He questioned the most basic things about the way school functions. Like, why did the school day have to be so long? All the rigid routines-- why do they have to learn in class periods? Why every day?

segments.speaker: Takeru Nagayoshi
segments.text: Sometimes, I just felt more like a gatekeeper to, like, archaic ways of learning and convening. I don't know, Chana, I just feel like the seal has been broken, and I don't-- and it's hard for me to imagine a world to go back to that magic.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Whoa. What seal has been broken? What does that mean?

segments.speaker: Takeru Nagayoshi
segments.text: The-- [SIGHS] what is the seal that has been broken? I think, our relationship to what school is.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's been two years since school buildings first closed. It's kind of hard to remember how impossible that seemed before it happened-- closing entire school buildings. School seemed like a fact, inevitable. If you're a kid, you go to school five days a week. It's inescapable.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But then, it wasn't anymore. Buildings closed for months, more than a year. This happened in lots of different ways across the country. It was worse for some, better for others. But talking with teachers and parents and kids, it's clear that school as they left it March 2020 does not look the same as the school they have now.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Classrooms still close. School buses don't come. Or teachers are out sick, or there aren't enough teachers. Some districts have just decided kids don't need to come in on Fridays now. In the state of Missouri, 1/4 of the school districts have now decided to switch to four days of school a week, instead of five.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Some kids stopped coming altogether. School had always been this solid object that now seems much less solid. So many of the people I've been speaking with are questioning the very premise of school, whether it's worth it, whether they need to show up every day, whether they need to be in a classroom.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's like everyone involved-- kids, parents, drivers, teachers, superintendents-- all realized at the same time, hey, this treadmill has an off switch. This place is not fact. School is not inevitable. Just listen to the way Mr. Nagayoshi talks about when school was inevitable, back before the pandemic, just a few years ago.

segments.speaker: Takeru Nagayoshi
segments.text: Sure, it was hard, and things were never perfect, but it was a different time. And I don't know if we can ever get back to that. I think it's a bygone era.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Like, the way we've done public school for more than a century?

segments.speaker: Takeru Nagayoshi
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: [CHUCKLES] It's gone?

segments.speaker: Takeru Nagayoshi
segments.text: I don't-- I think it is.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Is it? Is school as we've known it over? Today, I want to bring you the stories of two kids who have drifted away from school. And we see what happens when they try to make their way back. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The last couple of months, I've been talking with principals, teachers, parents, and kids about school and what's changed for them two years into a pandemic. And I keep returning to that question-- have schools fundamentally changed? One of the people I've been checking in with, on and off for a while now, is a woman named MJ and her daughter, Neeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: They're a family of three. MJ is a single parent. Neeah is her youngest, and she has an older daughter, who's grown. They're mixed-race, live in Michigan with a French bulldog. During the pandemic, MJ and Neeah constructed a brand-new and very unusual life with one another. And seeing how much has changed for them, where they ended up after two years of pandemic school, that, maybe more than anyone else I've spoken with, made me feel like, whoa, maybe school as we once knew it truly is over.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So here's Act One, Big Mother Is Watching. It begins, of course, when the schools closed two years ago.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: Oh, my god. You want to talk about stress? Man.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What happened?

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: Oh, yeah. It just-- like, what do you do?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: MJ is a building engineer. She had to go to work. She supervises all the maintenance for buildings she works in around Detroit-- make sure the boilers, lighting, carpentry are all attended to. So at first, she just brought Neeah to work.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: It was fun, you know what I mean? She didn't get in my way, running around while I'm cleaning up, you know, that area that I have to. So you know, I rode the wave as long as I could.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: When her boss made it clear that this was not a long-term arrangement, MJ dropped Neeah with an aunt, then a friend, a babysitter. A neighbor took her for a week.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: You know, even if it's just a day, OK, exactly how long can they help? You know, throw them money. How much can you afford? Absolutely nothing, but we'll make it work anyway. It's a never-- it's a whole thing. It's exhausting, mentally. Exhausting, OK?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And it was months. MJ had a new thought. Neeah was nine years old. She could prepare food herself, get herself dressed. A lot of parents leave kids her age at home alone. But MJ hadn't before, certainly not all day. And she did not want to now, but she had to go to work. She'd be 10 minutes away. She could come home at lunch to check in. Neeah would be on Zoom all day, with a teacher from school.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: A while back, a friend had recommended security cameras when MJ moved into a new house. MJ ordered a couple. Neeah stayed home alone. MJ left, telling herself, I've got the cameras.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: I could see her in different areas of the house. And I have an alarm system that, if any window or doors opened, it alerts the police and makes a really loud noise. And you know, depending on the area of the house that Neeah's in, she knows what the escape route is and what the emergency plan is.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: You know, it's not something that I wanted to do. I wasn't happy to do it, but I can see my kid. You know, like I said, I got a friend behind me, my neighbor across-- the old lady across the street. Gotta love them, you know?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: When did you first start watching?

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: Right away.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Oh, really?

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: No, no, right away. Oh, god, yeah. No. My kid's got to be home by herself? I got to keep my eyes on the camera.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: MJ went to work and propped the phone up next to her, all day. If she had to walk, she'd hold the phone in front of her, and she'd watch as Neeah ate breakfast, signed on to school. When MJ couldn't have eyes on the phone, she'd put it in her pocket and put headphones in to listen.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: It's never not been a distraction. I'm always busy, but I have to keep my daughter in my ear, because she's home by herself. You know? So it did interfere with work, you know. It's what I do. Like, I'm on a ladder, trying to change lights, and you know, I've got my phone.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: Like, I'll set it up somewhere. I'll put, like, the phone in my pocket, put my earphones in, so I can at least hear. And if, you know, something sounds awry, like if I hear a bang, I'd pull my phone out, look at the camera real quick. But I'm always listening.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: On a ladder?

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: Always listening.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I hate this picture, MJ.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You're standing on a ladder, looking at your phone.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: Changing a fluorescent light in a hallway. And yeah, and you'll hear-- now, if you subtract, da-da-da-dah, and like you hear the kids. They're so loud. Yeah, it's bad. It was bad. [CHUCKLES]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: MJ watched as much as she could, listened when she couldn't. She was monitoring to keep Neeah safe. But as she watched, MJ started to notice some other things.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: Oh. [CHUCKLES] Like, I'm very big on eating in my living room. Like, I don't like to-- I don't like when you eat or drink in my living room. And I've caught her so many times eating and drinking in the living room and setting it next to the laptop. And I don't like my dog on the couch all the time, because he licks his paw, and then licks the couch. And it's just gross. And she'll let him on the couch.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: MJ told me, on the app, you can see everything. And there's a big button right there-- Microphone. If you press it, your voice will blast into the room, sounding sort of like a loud walkie-talkie. I asked--

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So did you use it?

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: Oh, oh, hell yeah. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Tell me.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: I would just hit my Microphone button, and I would catch her watching TV all the time. I'd be like, turn the TV off. What did I say? Getting up, playing with the dog, playing with the cat, back and forth. Like, no, sit your self down, and do your work.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Neeah would get herself a drink, bring it to the living room-- Microphone.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: Neeah, you know you're not supposed to have that by the laptop. You need to go put it in the kitchen. Neeah, quit playing with the dog and focus. Turn off the TV. You're not supposed to have the TV on. If you're going to listen to the music, no lyrics. Yeah, it's just constant redirection and correction, over and over.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What were the ones that you said the most often?

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: All of 'em.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The app apparently can also record. MJ told me, yeah, you can capture moments on there.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: Or take pictures.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Did you do that?

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: Oh, I've recorded. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Why?

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: Just so I can go back and show her her behavior. Like, flipping, doing cartwheels, oh, yeah. Mm-hmm, I'll go, oh, yeah. Oh, you're doing cartwheels? OK.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Did she ever cover up the cameras?

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: She tried to turn one before, yes, so I couldn't watch her watching TV.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: So she would always definitely feel like I was spying on her. Stop spying on me! [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It sounds like you were.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: I mean, was I spying on her, or was I making sure she was OK? You know, tomato, to-ma-to.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Hi, Neeah.

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: Hello.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: How are you?

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Neeah told me she jumped the first few times her mom's voice appeared in the room with her. Other times, she says it was just confusing. Her teacher was talking, and her mom was talking. She felt like, wait, who's telling me to do something right now? A version of this happened as Neeah and I talked. MJ was sitting right next to her on the bed, jumping in here and there.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Is she the same mom through the cameras?

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: Yeah, sometimes. But through the camera, she's more of a helicopter parent. Make sure you get your chores done before I get home, or I'm going to be mad, or you're going to be grounded. And I would always want to watch TV, but she's like, no, turn off the TV, turn off the music, you got to focus. No chewing gum. Make sure you're paying attention.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She said she'd talk to you about your drinks and the dog a lot, too.

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: Are you supposed to drink by the laptop?

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: Are you supposed to eat by the laptop?

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: There you go. [CHUCKLES]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: Yeah, it seems more different over the camera, actually, because-- yeah, much more of a micromanager on the cameras than in person.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She's micromanaging this conversation.

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: Yes, she is.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: Yeah, I am. Sorry.

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: She's doing a good job at it.

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: [MJ LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You can tell MJ and Neeah like each other. And even with this setup, the cameras watching Neeah, they started calling it, "the system." It didn't strain their relationship. If anything, the system made them closer.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: When Neeah hadn't heard her mom's voice for a while over the cameras, she'd FaceTime her mom, see what she was up to. She started to learn about her mom's day. She learned her habits. Neeah told me she got to the point where she could anticipate which things would trigger her mom's voice appearing in the room. Like, Neeah would turn on the TV, and as she was doing it--

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: I'm like, oh, god, I know she's about to come on the camera, tell me to focus, get off the TV.

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: [MJ LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: That's funny.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You would know ahead of time.

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: Yeah, I would know ahead of time.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Did it stop you from doing the thing that she didn't want you to do?

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: Um, no. Mm-mm. No. I'm still sassy. I still got some attitude.

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: [MJ LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: In in-person school in the classroom, this was a problem. Neeah loves to talk. She's a chatty kid, and she'd get in trouble for talking in class, distracting other kids, not keeping her hands to herself. MJ worried about it. She would get calls from school saying Neeah was acting out today. Neeah was suspended.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Parent-teacher conferences were often a lot of, "Neeah's a great kid, but she has a hard time focusing." But now, the space between home and school had collapsed. Instead of hearing about Neeah second-hand, MJ was watching. And she says it was kind of amazing. Neeah was curious. She was hard-working.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: She would ask questions. Like, if she didn't know, she'd raise her hand, because you'd see her on camera-- raise her hand, waiting patiently and quietly. Whereas Neeah, she usually-- she interrupts. Let's just be real.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: Not saying she never interrupted, but like, I just-- she was raising her hand, waiting patiently, asked questions, gave the right answer. And it's like, I don't ever get to see that. You know what I mean? I don't get to hear the good stuff all the time.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: That's really kind of special that you got to see her that way.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Like, to see her strengths and what she's capable of.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah. Absolutely. And her weaknesses, you know. I see the distraction. She is easily distracted. You know, it is hard, and just-- well, it's difficult for her to stay focused, you know? But when she gets into her groove, you know, she stays in it. And she just does amazing things. Yeah.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: I'm glad I got to see this side of my kid that they haven't seen, that I haven't seen. And it's like, this is who she is. I've had that moment, like wow, this is who my kid is.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I'd never heard of someone doing this-- MJ's system, using security cameras in your house to monitor kids doing remote school, while you have to go to work. It seemed extreme to me, but then I considered all the other arrangements and half-solutions I've heard parents devising to replace what school provided-- a free, dependable place to drop your kids.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Parents who brought kids to their jobs at restaurants planted them at a table in the corner, while they worked their shift and hoped nobody in management asked, whose kid is that? Moms who put their children in empty hotel rooms to do remote school while they cleaned the other rooms down the hall. Parents who cut back on their hours or quit their jobs, took night shifts, so they could stay up all day with their kids doing Zoom school.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Families that moved their entire lives to new cities that were cheaper or closer to a grandma who could look after the kids. MJ had a system that did not require her to depend on anyone else. The system was never late, or stuck in traffic, or sick, or too tired. It's kind of ingenious. School was not reliable. The system was entirely within her control.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Did you know other people who were doing this?

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: No. I mean, if other moms are out there not wanting to say nothing, I get it. But, whew, there's not that panic of what so many other parents had to face that didn't have a system. I feel like I should do like an infomercial or something, you know-- (LAUGHING) for the system of security cameras and things like that.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: MJ
segments.text: I made it work. [LAUGHS] I made it work.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And then, schools reopened. After 11 months of constant contact with her mom, zero separation, Neeah went back to a school building.

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: I had butterflies the entire time I was there. I'm like, oh, my god. What if I do something wrong? What if I get suspended today? And like, what if I don't make it through fourth grade?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: Just a whole day of butterflies, and--

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: Yeah, in the snap of a finger, I'm like, oh, crap. And my mom's not going to be here to be-- like, be here to watch over me, tell me to focus. Like, how am I going to do this? How am I going to do that without her telling me what to do? And that's when I started getting these panic attacks. Like--

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You started getting panic attacks when you went back to school?

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I'm sorry to hear that.

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: Mm-hmm. One of them was really bad, because I was in a panic attack for about 10, 15 minutes, because someone made me mad, really mad, kind of to the point where I started to cry a little bit. And then, I asked the substitute teacher if I can go to the bathroom. And then that's when it happened.

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: Like, I completely stopped. My heart stopped. My hands were shaking completely. I couldn't even talk. And then, thank god, this teacher, Ms. Murf let me sit in her room for a little bit, cool down, and go back to my room.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You know, when you send a preschooler to their first day of school, that first big separation? And it's so hard, but you can never really know exactly what it's like for the kid, because they're so little. They can't really articulate it. But here is a fourth-grader who can.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Neeah says she missed knowing where her mom was. She missed her voice in the room. When things happened at school, when a kid said something mean, or she didn't understand the teacher, she wanted her mom there to take care of it, to protect her.

segments.speaker: Neeah
segments.text: Like, how I said she was talking a lot on the cameras?

segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Chana Joffe-Walt, sitting in for Ira Glass. segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: This episode is also about that feeling, a slow-moving unraveling in schools. We are now in the third consecutive school year disrupted by COVID-- disruptions that have at times undone even the most basic foundational part of what school is, like the idea that kids go to school every day. Attendance is down. Enrollment is down.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I remember back when schools first closed two years ago, there were kids who just disappeared. I saw a report in the fall of 2020 that estimated three million kids were out of touch with school. segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt

segments.text: So much of our conversation about schools right now, our ideas about what schools need, what needs to happen to help kids catch up, to get back to normal, usually comes from the perspective of teachers, parents, adults. I want you to hear Maricela's version of this, to hear what it's been like for one of the millions of kids during the pandemic who just stopped attending school-- all the details that matter to her, the stuff that is at eye-level to a kid, stuff adults don't always think to focus on.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It was not a blip for Maricela, it was epic. A lot happened. First, her mom lost her job. Then, her grandparents got sick. And while they were in Mexico, they lost their apartment in Los Angeles. The manager said they'd abandoned it. When they came back to Los Angeles, Maricela's aunt said they could stay with her.

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: We all had our schedules, like, who does this, who does that. For example, like, we would wake up, and we would sleep in the living room. We would pick up, we would vacuum the whole living room. We would have to wash the dishes, cook, and then wash those dishes, and broom the kitchen, clean the table after we're done eating, and then clean the bathroom, if it's dirty.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Her cousins' kids, though, her aunt's kids-- Maricela says they hardly did anything. She's the oldest in her family. It's her and a younger brother and sister. So a lot of the chores fell to her. It wasn't fair.

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: And I couldn't tell them anything, because they're snitches. And they told their parents everything about what they do. So I would just ignore it.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It got tense in the apartment. And sometime in the middle of what would have been Maricela's seventh-grade school year, her family moved into their truck. They'd drive to the park she always played at and grab a spot every night. In the daytime, they had a routine. Her younger brother and sister would sleep in the back.

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: They would wake up, like, around 9:00. We would go get breakfast while they were sleeping. We would wake-- we would go park at the park again, and then they would wake up. We would fix the seats, and then they would sit down and eat breakfast.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And then, what would happen? What would you do the rest of the day?

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: And then, we would go to my mom's-- to my cousin's house, and we would shower there. We had bathrooms at the park. And to brush our teeth, we'd just brush them like-- we would go to the bathroom, take a water bottle, toothpaste, and my toothbrush, and we would brush them in there.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I talked to Maricela's mom. She confirmed the basics. She lost her job when the pandemic hit, the apartment. They went to Mexico to care for her folks. But she didn't want to do an interview or get into any of this in detail.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So I don't know much about where her head was at or what shaped all the different choices she had to make during that time. She wanted to let Maricela share her experience. When they were staying in the truck, Maricela's mom called LA Family Housing. A caseworker got them a place in a hotel. That's where they're living now.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And then, the caseworker asked where Maricela wanted to register for school. I don't know if she asked or if she told her she had to. GALS is 40 minutes, in traffic, from the hotel. Maybe somewhere closer, she asked? No, Maricela said. She'd prefer to go back to the school she knows.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's funny, when you think about it, that very basic idea that school is where you go as a kid, the thing the rest of life revolves around, it took centuries to establish. It took laws, and social movements, and fiery speeches to establish a sprawling compulsory public education system. But it only took a few months-- weeks, even, with Maricela-- for that idea to be completely undone.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And when it was, when school disappeared from Maricela's life, all the other things-- more immediate, huge dramas-- came in and filled the space. Her mom lost her job. They lived in a truck. She sold candy in the park. Her cousins were snitches. Her family died.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She can talk about all of that for hours. But when I asked Maricela, what about school, she just sort of drifts to some other topic. Not that she doesn't want to talk about it, it almost felt like she didn't remember when the pandemic closed schools. It didn't register.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What did you do in sixth grade when schools closed?

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: Um, in sixth grade, when school closed, I didn't finish sixth grade.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Why? I would ask, over and over. They closed schools, she'd say. But what about online school? No. Why? I don't know.

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: It was-- because I wasn't in school at that time.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Why weren't you in school at that time?

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: I don't know.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Did you want to be in school?

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: No. Because I knew that I couldn't hang out with Valeria.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Valeria. Valeria was Maricela's best friend at school. She lived in her building. The vague fog Maricela has when I ask her about school evaporated instantly when the conversation turned to Valeria in sixth grade.

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: No, I met her-- OK, so when she came from Mexico, she would, like, go to my house a lot. We lived in the same building, and she would go, like, at 6:00 in the morning, and we would come on our way to school together. And we were, like, really close friends that-- this one time, she was knocking at my door, and I opened it, and then we made breakfast together, and then we served--

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Maricela became so specific when she talked about Valeria, in that kid way where she's living it in real time, where every detail of a story is shared and assigned exactly equal weight. She knocked. I opened the door. We made breakfast. Here's who came. Here's where we sat. Here's what we ate.

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: --like a tortilla. And then you crack an egg on top. And then, we sliced, like, tomatoes and onions, and we put it on the top. She went to her house, and she got clothes. And she showered in my mom's bathroom while I showered in mine. And then--

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: They went out walking, and they ran into Maricela's aunt, who gave her some cash. They went to the store. Maricela snuck to the side and bought something special.

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: They were, like, little silver hearts that come apart, and they said, "best friends."

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Like one of those best-friend hearts, broken heart?

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: Yeah, but it was like a keychain thing, and we both had it, like, on our backpack. And when we came to the school both together, we were, like, so close. And we would hang out with the other girls, but there was, like, always a space with the other girls.

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: But me and her were, like, always next to each other. We were, like, really best friends. And then, we would go to the bathroom, and she would wait for me, like, outside the stall. And then she would go in, and I would wait for her.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: March 2020, schools closed and upended the lives of millions of families. But again, that's not what Maricela remembers of this time. March 2020, the day before Maricela went to Mexico, what she remembers is that she had a picnic with Valeria at the Valley Plaza Park. Their families came. They ate Pollo Loco.

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: That day, it was her birthday. And I had to tell her that we were leaving. But her brother-- her brother knew before her, but we were supposed to surprise her. But when we were singing Happy Birthday, he told her. And then her eyes got kind of watery.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What about you?

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: I wanted to cry.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Did you?

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Maricela told Valeria she'd see her soon, but she never did. Valeria's family had been trying to make it work in LA, but struggled in those early months of the pandemic, and decided to move back to Ciudad Juarez. That was the last time they saw each other.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: How does it feel to walk through the halls now?

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Knowing what the last year and a half was for Maricela, that it was not a blip, but a long time for a 12-year-old, full of huge experiences, I consider how brave it is what she's doing-- returning to this place that disappeared from her life, coming back after losing family members, her apartment, moving between countries, returning without knowing anything about what she's missed and without Valeria.

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: I was nervous, scared. I was like nervous, like, who I will see here. I go to the school, and then I leave. And then I come back, and they just stare at you the whole time. And I get nervous when they stare at me.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You get nervous when they stare at you?

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: It's, like, weird.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What does it feel like?

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: It feels like a bunch of cameras watching me.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It does kind of seem like that. I watch as Maricela moves through the rest of her school day. She gets a lot of stares. She looks very nervous and very lost.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: People were accusing Hamilton of being what's called a monarchist. Remember King George III?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: In history class, the teacher does a lot of, remember when we learned about blah, blah, blah? Like, who can tell me what we know about the monarchy? Who remembers? The elites-- what do we mean by elites? You guys remember? Maricela, of course, does not remember.

segments.speaker: Teacher 2
segments.text: OK, so we're going to do quite a bit of reading today. All right. 109, Alabama, is everybody there?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: In English class, they read a novel written in verse, and then they have to write a response on an online platform. Maricela can't figure out how to submit her response. She's frustrated, but does not ask for help, does not know about the monarchy. She does not know how to use the online learning platform, and she does not speak to anyone.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She's here. She's finally in the building, but she's still really far away. I felt that deeply, watching her in math. They're playing a game. Everyone has to get up and split it into two groups, but Maricela doesn't move.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She's sitting in the back row, and she stays completely still, backpack propped on her desk, looking panicked as the other kids get up and sort themselves into teams. She's wearing a mic clipped to her shirt. She's too far from anyone else for them to hear what she's saying, but I can.

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: [GROANS] My stomach hurts.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The teacher notices that Maricela hasn't moved. And for the first time in hours, someone addresses her directly, tells her, you too. Come on.

segments.speaker: Teacher 3
segments.text: You, too, pick a group. This one or that one?

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: What if I can't play?

segments.speaker: Teacher 3
segments.text: You can play. It's just math.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's just math, the teacher says. But it is clearly not just math to Maricela. I keep waiting for someone to talk to her, to ask her something. What's going on with you? Where were you? What do you need?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But school, day-to-day school, is not really set up for that. Her teachers will assess where Maricela is academically. And there's an aide in classes that could help her one-on-one, sometimes. But mostly, school is like this.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: This interaction with the math teacher, it lasts 11 seconds. She locks her eyes on Maricela, Maricela shakes her head. And then another kid jumps in front of the teacher, and the room of 25 people moves forward.

segments.speaker: Teacher 3
segments.text: So I'm going to give you a question. Whoever answers the question first gets to come up here and write there, either their circle or their X. OK?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: School is a machine that is designed to move forward. Kids move class-to-class, grade-to-grade. The machine does not stop. It's not designed to go back in time, to meet Maricela where she's at right now, which is at the back of the classroom, hiding behind a backpack, as her classmates enthusiastically compete to solve a math equation.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: [STUDENTS YELLING EXCITEDLY]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Out of all the awkward moments I saw that day, this one was the hardest to watch, because you can feel the conveyor belt of school moving forward. I could see Maricela's panic that she could not figure out how to jump on.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And then, I see her try. Right before lunch, Maricela's standing in the hallway nervously digging through her backpack, other kids streaming past her to the lunch tables outside.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And then, all of a sudden, she calls out to another kid.

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: Arecilli, mira.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She says, Arecilli, look, and opens up her bag. Arecilli is a tall, quiet girl in pink, who's been moving through the whole day in a pack of three-- three girls who, I'm told, have all recently arrived at the school from Mexico. Maricela starts showing Arecilli all the candy, and snacks, and lotion in her backpack.

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: Oh, look, and I have these. And I have-- look, and I have these. I have Bath and Body Works, too. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Now, the three girls are all leaning in over her backpack, giggling and slowly moving through the hall toward lunch up ahead of me. And a sixth-grader quickly replaces Maricela at my side, tells me she's been on TV, so I might recognize her.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Have you seen a commercial where a dad's fixing a purple Jeep with his daughter?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: No. Is that you?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You're the daughter?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Yeah. And do you know the show, Henry Danger? OK. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: After disappointing this child star, I spot Maricela outside. She's in line for lunch, and she's with Arecilli and her friends. They're a nervous-looking pack, looking around like something bad could happen, not really talking. But they're a pack. Maricela seems OK for the first time in the whole day, actually, excited.

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: Hanging out with Arecilli-- she's like Valeria.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: Mm-hmm. They speak the same.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Like, the way that they speak sounds the same?

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: Mm-hmm. And they kind of look the same.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It seems to me like an effort to jump back on the conveyor belt, that Maricela's trying to replicate what she had here before that mattered to her, trying to make a new school friend, who apparently is not dissimilar to her old school friend.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Arecilli looks like her?

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: Mm-hmm. It was the tall, skinny girl that was with me right now.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Do you think you guys will become as close?

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: Mm, I don't know, because, we're already in eighth grade. And then, when she leaves, I'm going to feel alone.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But you'd have eighth grade together.

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: Mm.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So you don't want to become close to her because, after eighth grade, you might not be together anymore?

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: Mm-hmm. That's why.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I get it. She can't go back. They can't be as close, because Maricela missed most of middle school. And middle school is almost over. She can't go back to sixth-grade math, just like she can't go back to her apartment.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And she definitely can't go back to Valeria. Everything is moving forward without her. Maricela watches Valeria online now, becoming a teenager without her.

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: I see her, like-- I see her stories, and she looks, like, way different.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: Like, she had, like, a little bit of freckles here, and they disappeared. And she had, like-- she put a nose piercing on. She's gonna-- I think she's gonna turn, like, 15.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What does it feel like to see her looking different?

segments.speaker: Maricela
segments.text: Um, it feels weird. She, like, dresses different. She used to wear, like, long sleeves and jeans. And now she wears, like, really ripped jeans. And she wears, like, cropped tops now. Actually, it's like, I miss her.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I don't know how schools are going to fit in kids like Maricela. There are so many of them-- not just the millions of kids who have become chronically absent or disappeared entirely, but the tens of millions of kids who fell behind in math and reading, the millions of kids suffering from anxiety, trauma, grief. What happens if they don't fit back in?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Maricela has been coming to school for six months now, but she doesn't always come. Her attendance is pretty spotty. Principal Vanessa Garza tells me Maricela is now three grades behind, but she will be promoted to ninth grade.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She won't be able to walk at graduation because of the attendance issues, but Ms. Vanessa thinks the shame of being held back would be the end of school for Maricela. And she has a better shot of finishing high school, if she can start earning credits toward graduation now. She'll keep moving forward.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I asked Maricela if she likes being back in school. She said, no, but she's going to keep trying.
